plainLanguage: Multiplication means a number of equal groups. 4 x 6 is four groups with six in each group.
expectedMethods: Draw or describe the equal groups
Build an array of rows and columns
Skip count by the group size
parentMethod: Recite the times tables until the fact is automatic.

plainLanguage: Division means splitting a total into equal groups, either asking how many groups or how many in each group.
expectedMethods: Share the total out one at a time into groups
Draw an array and find the missing side
Ask what times the divisor gives the total
parentMethod: Short division, the bus stop method, done digit by digit.

plainLanguage: Word problems where the numbers are joined by multiplying or dividing, up to 100.
expectedMethods: Draw a bar model showing the parts and the whole
Write the equation with a box for the unknown
Act the situation out with counters
parentMethod: Look for a keyword in the question and pick the operation it suggests.

plainLanguage: Finding the missing number in something like 8 x ? = 48.
expectedMethods: Use the matching division fact
Count up in groups until you reach the total
Use an array with one side unknown
parentMethod: Divide the total by the number you know.

plainLanguage: Multiplication can be reordered and regrouped without changing the answer, which makes hard facts easier.
expectedMethods: Break one factor into friendlier parts, so 7 x 6 becomes 5 x 6 plus 2 x 6
Swap the order to use the easier fact
Use a known fact to reach a nearby one
parentMethod: Memorise each fact separately as its own item.

plainLanguage: Division is a multiplication with one factor missing.
expectedMethods: Rewrite the division as a multiplication with a box
Use the related fact family
parentMethod: Treat division as its own separate procedure.

plainLanguage: Knowing multiplication and division facts within 100 quickly and accurately.
expectedMethods: Derive an unknown fact from a known one
Use doubling and halving
Practise the facts in fact families
parentMethod: Rote recitation of the tables in order.

plainLanguage: Two-step word problems, where you have to do one thing and then another.
expectedMethods: Draw a bar model for each step
Write an equation with a letter for the unknown
Estimate first, then check the answer is reasonable
parentMethod: Work through the sentence left to right in the order the numbers appear.

plainLanguage: Rounding a number to the nearest ten or hundred.
expectedMethods: Place the number on a number line between the two nearest tens or hundreds
Decide which one it is closer to
parentMethod: Look at the next digit, five or more rounds up, four or less rounds down.

plainLanguage: Adding and subtracting numbers up to 1000 fluently.
expectedMethods: Partition into hundreds, tens and ones and add each part
Count on or back in jumps on an empty number line
Use a written column method once the parts are understood
parentMethod: Column addition and subtraction with carrying and borrowing.

plainLanguage: Multiplying a single digit by a multiple of ten, like 6 x 40.
expectedMethods: Multiply by the single digit, then by ten
Think of it as six groups of four tens
parentMethod: Multiply the non-zero digits and add the zero on the end.

plainLanguage: A fraction like 3/4 is three copies of one part when a whole is cut into four equal parts.
expectedMethods: Fold or shade a shape into equal parts
Name the unit fraction first, then count copies of it
parentMethod: Read the top number and the bottom number as two separate numbers.

plainLanguage: A fraction is a number with a place on the number line, not just a piece of a shape.
expectedMethods: Mark the whole from 0 to 1 and cut it into equal parts
Count unit fractions along the line
parentMethod: Think of fractions only as slices of a pizza or a cake.

plainLanguage: Two different fractions can be the same size, and fractions can be compared when the whole is the same.
expectedMethods: Line both fractions up on the same number line
Use a fraction wall to see which is longer
Find a common way of cutting the whole
parentMethod: Compare the numbers on the bottom, or cross multiply.

plainLanguage: Area is found by covering a shape with unit squares, which is why length times width works.
expectedMethods: Tile the rectangle with unit squares and count them
Split a shape into two rectangles and add the areas
parentMethod: Apply the formula length times width without drawing anything.

plainLanguage: Perimeter is the distance all the way around the edge, area is the space inside.
expectedMethods: Walk a finger round the edge and add each side
Compare two shapes with the same perimeter and different areas
parentMethod: Use the formula for perimeter and the formula for area and keep them separate.

plainLanguage: Reading 35 = 5 x 7 as a comparison: 35 is five times as many as seven.
expectedMethods: Draw two bars, one five times the length of the other
Say the sentence out loud as a comparison
parentMethod: Read the equation as an instruction to multiply.

plainLanguage: Word problems about one amount being a number of times another amount.
expectedMethods: Draw a comparison bar model
Write the equation with a letter for the unknown
parentMethod: Pick the operation from a keyword in the sentence.

plainLanguage: Multi-step word problems, including deciding what to do with a remainder.
expectedMethods: Bar model the whole situation before calculating
Estimate first and check the answer is sensible
Say in words what the remainder means here
parentMethod: Calculate in the order the numbers appear and give the remainder as r.

plainLanguage: Factors, multiples, and whether a number is prime or composite.
expectedMethods: Build rectangles of the number to find factor pairs
List factor pairs in order from one upwards
parentMethod: Test each number in turn to see if it divides.

plainLanguage: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
expectedMethods: Use a place value chart and move a digit one column
Exchange ten of one unit for one of the next
parentMethod: Name the columns from memory: ones, tens, hundreds.

plainLanguage: Reading, writing and comparing multi-digit numbers in digits, words and expanded form.
expectedMethods: Write the number in expanded form as a sum of place values
Compare digit by digit from the left
parentMethod: Compare by length first, then read left to right.

plainLanguage: Rounding a multi-digit whole number to any place.
expectedMethods: Place the number between the two nearest round numbers on a line
Ask which of the two it sits closer to
parentMethod: Look at the digit to the right and round up on five.

plainLanguage: Adding and subtracting multi-digit numbers fluently.
expectedMethods: Partition both numbers and add each place
Use an empty number line to count on
Use the column method once regrouping is understood
parentMethod: Column addition and subtraction with carrying and borrowing.

plainLanguage: Multiplying up to four digits by one digit, and two digits by two digits.
expectedMethods: Use an area model, splitting each number by place value
Use partial products and add them
Use the grid method
parentMethod: Long multiplication in columns, with carried digits above.

plainLanguage: Dividing up to four digits by one digit, with remainders.
expectedMethods: Partial quotients, taking away easy chunks of the divisor
Use an area model with the divisor as one side
Estimate with a friendly multiple first
parentMethod: Long division, the bring-down method, or short division at the bus stop.

plainLanguage: Two fractions are equivalent when the whole is cut into more parts but the same amount is taken.
expectedMethods: Cut each part of a fraction strip into the same number of smaller parts
Use a fraction wall to find equal lengths
Multiply top and bottom by the same number once the model is understood
parentMethod: Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.

plainLanguage: Comparing two fractions with different numerators and denominators.
expectedMethods: Compare each to a half as a benchmark
Rewrite both with the same denominator
Place both on the same number line
parentMethod: Cross multiply and compare the two products.

plainLanguage: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator, by counting unit fractions.
expectedMethods: Count in unit fractions along a number line
Join fraction strips end to end
Decompose the fraction into a sum of unit fractions
parentMethod: Add the tops and keep the bottom the same.

plainLanguage: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number, understood as repeated addition of the fraction.
expectedMethods: Repeat the fraction on a number line
Show the whole number as that many copies of the fraction
parentMethod: Multiply the numerator by the whole number.

plainLanguage: Adding fractions with denominators of ten and a hundred, which leads into decimals.
expectedMethods: Use a hundred grid, ten columns shaded for each tenth
Rewrite tenths as hundredths before adding
parentMethod: Convert both to hundredths and add the numerators.

plainLanguage: Writing fractions with denominators of ten and a hundred as decimals.
expectedMethods: Shade a hundred grid and read it two ways
Place both forms on the same number line
parentMethod: Move the decimal point the right number of places.

plainLanguage: Comparing decimals to hundredths, where the number of digits does not decide the size.
expectedMethods: Line the numbers up on a place value chart
Put both on a number line between the same two whole numbers
Shade both on hundred grids and compare the shading
parentMethod: Compare place by place after lining up the decimal points.

plainLanguage: Using formulas for the area and perimeter of a rectangle in real situations.
expectedMethods: Draw the rectangle and label both dimensions
Tile or partition before reaching for the formula
parentMethod: Apply the formula for whichever one the question names.

plainLanguage: An angle is an amount of turn, measured in degrees, not a length.
expectedMethods: Turn a pencil through the angle to feel the rotation
Compare the angle to a right angle
parentMethod: Read the number off the protractor.

plainLanguage: Angles that meet add together, so a missing angle can be found by subtracting.
expectedMethods: Draw the angles meeting at a point and label the known parts
Write an addition equation with the unknown as a letter
parentMethod: Subtract the known angles from 180 or 360.

plainLanguage: Brackets say which part of a calculation to do first.
expectedMethods: Work out the innermost bracket first and rewrite the line
Read the expression aloud as a sentence
parentMethod: Follow the order of operations, brackets then powers then times and divide then add and subtract.

plainLanguage: Writing an expression for a situation without working it out.
expectedMethods: Write the expression, then say in words what it represents
Compare two expressions without calculating either
parentMethod: Calculate a value straight away rather than leaving it as an expression.

plainLanguage: A digit is worth ten times the place to its right and one tenth of the place to its left.
expectedMethods: Use a place value chart that runs past the decimal point
Multiply and divide by ten and watch the digits shift
parentMethod: Move the decimal point left or right.

plainLanguage: Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten, and what happens to the zeros.
expectedMethods: Shift the digits along a place value chart
Write the power of ten out in full first
parentMethod: Add or remove zeros, or move the decimal point.

plainLanguage: Reading, writing and comparing decimals to thousandths.
expectedMethods: Write the decimal in expanded form as tenths, hundredths and thousandths
Compare on a place value chart, left to right
Place both on a number line between the same two tenths
parentMethod: Line up the decimal points and compare column by column.

plainLanguage: Rounding decimals to any place.
expectedMethods: Find the two nearest values on a number line and see which is closer
Say which two tenths or hundredths the number sits between
parentMethod: Look at the next digit and round up on five.

plainLanguage: Multiplying multi-digit whole numbers fluently.
expectedMethods: Area model split by place value
Partial products written out and added
The standard algorithm once the partial products are understood
parentMethod: Long multiplication in columns.

plainLanguage: Dividing with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors.
expectedMethods: Partial quotients, subtracting friendly multiples of the divisor
Area model with the divisor as one side
Estimate with a rounded divisor first
parentMethod: Long division with bring-down steps.

plainLanguage: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing decimals to hundredths.
expectedMethods: Use a hundred grid or base ten blocks for the operation
Estimate with whole numbers before calculating
Relate the decimal calculation to the matching whole number one
parentMethod: Line up the decimal points, or count the decimal places in the question.

plainLanguage: Adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators by finding a common way to cut the whole.
expectedMethods: Cut both fraction strips into the same size parts
Use a common denominator found from the two denominators
Show both on the same number line before adding
parentMethod: Find the lowest common denominator, convert both, then add the numerators.

plainLanguage: Word problems that add or subtract fractions, including checking the answer is sensible.
expectedMethods: Bar model the whole and the parts
Estimate with benchmarks like a half before calculating
parentMethod: Convert to a common denominator and calculate.

plainLanguage: A fraction is a division: 3/4 is three divided by four.
expectedMethods: Share three things between four people and see what each gets
Read the fraction bar aloud as divided by
parentMethod: Treat the fraction bar as separate from division.

plainLanguage: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as taking a part of a part.
expectedMethods: Fold or shade an area model twice, once each way
Say the calculation aloud as a part of a part
parentMethod: Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.

plainLanguage: Multiplying by a number less than one makes the result smaller, and this is not a special case.
expectedMethods: Compare the size of the answer to the starting number before calculating
Show the scaling on a number line
parentMethod: Multiply and notice afterwards that the answer got smaller.

plainLanguage: Real world problems that multiply fractions and mixed numbers.
expectedMethods: Bar model the situation before choosing an operation
Estimate the answer with benchmarks first
parentMethod: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions and multiply.

plainLanguage: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number and a whole number by a unit fraction.
expectedMethods: Ask how many of the divisor fit into the dividend
Draw the division on a number line
Act it out with a real quantity
parentMethod: Invert the second fraction and multiply.

plainLanguage: Volume is found by filling a solid with unit cubes.
expectedMethods: Build or picture the layers of unit cubes
Count one layer then multiply by the number of layers
parentMethod: Apply the formula length times width times height.

plainLanguage: A ratio compares two quantities by how many times one fits the other, not by how far apart they are.
expectedMethods: Draw a tape diagram with one bar per part
Build a ratio table by scaling both quantities together
Say the ratio aloud as for every this, that
parentMethod: Write the ratio as a fraction and simplify.

plainLanguage: A unit rate is how much of one quantity goes with exactly one of the other.
expectedMethods: Scale a ratio table down until one column reads one
Use a double number line
parentMethod: Divide the first number by the second.

plainLanguage: Using ratio and rate reasoning for real problems, including percentages and unit conversion.
expectedMethods: Ratio table with both quantities scaled together
Double number line with percent on one line and amount on the other
Find one percent first, then scale
parentMethod: Set up a proportion and cross multiply.

plainLanguage: Dividing a fraction by a fraction, understood as how many of these fit into that.
expectedMethods: Ask how many of the divisor fit inside the dividend
Draw both on the same number line
Use a common denominator and divide the numerators
parentMethod: Keep, change, flip: invert the second fraction and multiply.

plainLanguage: Dividing multi-digit numbers fluently.
expectedMethods: Partial quotients with friendly multiples
Estimate with rounded numbers first
parentMethod: Long division with bring-down steps.

plainLanguage: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing multi-digit decimals fluently.
expectedMethods: Estimate with whole numbers before calculating
Relate the decimal calculation to the whole number one
parentMethod: Line up the points, or count decimal places at the end.

plainLanguage: Greatest common factor and least common multiple, and using them to rewrite sums.
expectedMethods: List factors or multiples systematically
Use prime factorisation and take what is shared
Use the distributive property to factor a sum
parentMethod: List multiples of each number until one appears in both lists.

plainLanguage: Negative numbers describe quantities in opposite directions from zero.
expectedMethods: Put the situation on a number line through zero
Describe the opposite in context, such as below sea level
parentMethod: Treat the minus sign as an instruction to subtract.

plainLanguage: Placing positive and negative rational numbers on a number line and in the coordinate plane.
expectedMethods: Locate the number on a horizontal number line through zero
Reflect a point across an axis and read the new coordinates
parentMethod: Read the sign and place it left or right of zero.

plainLanguage: Ordering negative numbers, where further left means smaller even when the digits look bigger.
expectedMethods: Order by position on the number line, left to right
Say the comparison in context, such as colder than
Separate size from order by comparing absolute values as well
parentMethod: Compare the digits and ignore the sign.

plainLanguage: Exponents are repeated multiplication, not repeated addition.
expectedMethods: Write the power out in full before evaluating
Say it aloud as this many copies multiplied
parentMethod: Multiply the base by the exponent.

plainLanguage: A letter in an expression stands for a quantity that can vary, not a label for an object.
expectedMethods: Say aloud what the letter counts, in units
Substitute a value and evaluate
Read the expression as a sentence
parentMethod: Use the first letter of the word as a shorthand for the object.

plainLanguage: Rewriting an expression into an equivalent one using the properties of operations.
expectedMethods: Use an area model to see the distributive property
Check equivalence by substituting a value into both
parentMethod: Expand the brackets and collect like terms.

plainLanguage: Solving an equation means finding the values that make both sides equal, and the equals sign means the same as.
expectedMethods: Use a balance model, doing the same to both sides
Substitute the candidate back in and check both sides
parentMethod: Move the number to the other side and change the sign.

plainLanguage: Using a letter to represent an unknown number in a real situation.
expectedMethods: Define the letter in a sentence before writing the equation
Write the equation directly from the situation
parentMethod: Set up the sum and solve it without naming the unknown.

plainLanguage: Solving equations of the form x plus p equals q, and p times x equals q.
expectedMethods: Use a bar model with the unknown as one part
Do the same operation to both sides and show each line
parentMethod: Move the term across the equals sign and change its sign.

plainLanguage: Area of triangles and quadrilaterals, built from the area of a rectangle.
expectedMethods: Cut and rearrange the shape into a rectangle
See a triangle as half of a rectangle around it
parentMethod: Apply the formula for each shape as a separate rule.
